chapterNote: A miktam of David, written when the Philistines seized him in Gath (cf. 1 Sam 21:10-15). David is at his lowest — a fugitive from Saul, now captured in enemy territory — and the psalm models trust under terror. Two refrains anchor it: 'in God I trust, I will not be afraid — what can flesh do to me?' (vv. 4, 11) and the striking image of God collecting His servant's tears in a bottle.

1.text: For the chief musician. To the tune of 'The Silent Dove of the Distant Lands.' A miktam of David, when the Philistines seized him in Gath. Be gracious to me, O God, for men pant after me to swallow me whole; all day long the assailant presses in and crushes me down.
1.amp: Be gracious to me, O God [chanan — show favor where none is deserved], for men pant after me to swallow me whole [sha'aph — they eagerly snap at me, like a predator after prey]; all day long the assailant presses in and crushes me down [lacham — wages war on me, harasses without let-up].
1.notes: Superscription — miktam (H4387), an obscure musical/literary term, perhaps 'engraved' or 'gold-set'; the historical setting is 1 Sam 21:10-15. chanan (H2603) = to show favor/grace; sha'aph (H7602) = to pant after / gasp for / eagerly seize; lacham (H3898) here = to fight against / press in war.

2.text: My watchers pant after me all day long; many fight against me from their high and arrogant ground.
2.amp: My watchers [shurer — those lying in wait, watching for an opening] pant after me all day long; many fight against me from their high and arrogant ground [marom — they look down on me from the heights of their pride].
2.notes: shurer (H8324) = to watch maliciously / lie in ambush; marom (H4791) = a high place — here, the pride of the attackers who position themselves above their target.

3.text: On the day I am afraid, I will put my trust in You.
3.amp: On the day I am afraid [yare — the fear is real, not denied], I will put my trust in You [batach — lean my whole weight on You as my refuge].
3.notes: yare (H3372) = to fear/be afraid; batach (H982) = to trust, lean upon, find shelter in. The verse does not pretend the fear away; it answers fear with deliberate trust.

4.text: In God, whose word I praise — in God I have placed my trust, and I will not be afraid. What can mere flesh do to me?
4.amp: In God [Elohim], whose word I praise [halal — I boast in it, loud and unashamed]; in God I have placed my trust, and I will not be afraid. What can mere flesh do to me [basar — creaturely, frail, soon-gone flesh]?
4.notes: halal (H1984) = to praise/boast loudly; basar (H1320) = flesh — the contrast is between the eternal God whose word can be trusted and the finite, mortal 'flesh' of the attackers. First instance of the psalm's refrain.

5.text: All day long they twist what I say; every thought they have toward me is bent on evil.
5.amp: All day long they twist what I say [atsab — they pain and distort my words]; every thought they have toward me is bent on evil [machashebah — calculated schemes, all running in one direction: my harm].
5.notes: atsab (H6087) = to grieve/hurt/twist with pain; machashebah (H4284) = thought/scheme/device — a deliberate plot, not a passing impulse.

6.text: They gather and lurk together, watching my every step, lying in wait to take my life.
6.amp: They gather and lurk together [gur — they stir each other up against me], watching my every step [shamar — they keep a hostile eye on my heel], lying in wait to take my life [nephesh — my very breath, the whole of who I am].
6.notes: gur (H1481) here = to gather in hostility / pick a quarrel; shamar (H8104) used negatively = to watch with intent to harm; nephesh (H5315) = soul/life/self.

7.text: Because of their wickedness, shall they escape? In Your anger, O God, cast down these peoples.
7.amp: Because of their wickedness, shall they escape [palat — shall they slip through, unjudged]? In Your anger, O God, cast down these peoples [yarad — bring them down from the high ground they presume to hold].
7.notes: palat (H6403) = to escape/slip away; yarad (H3381) = to descend, be brought down. The psalmist appeals not to private revenge but to God's justice — the only Judge who can be trusted to rule rightly.

8.text: You Yourself keep count of my wanderings; gather my tears into Your bottle — are they not written down in Your book?
8.amp: You Yourself keep count of my wanderings [nod — the fugitive's tossings, every restless step]; gather my tears into Your bottle [no'd — the leather wineskin, cherished and stored]; are they not written down in Your book [sepher — the ledger of remembrance]?
8.notes: Hebrew wordplay: nod (H5112, wandering) and no'd (H4997, leather bottle) sound almost identical. The image is unforgettable: every restless mile David walks as a fugitive, God counts; every tear he sheds, God collects and stores like rare wine. This is intimate, almost tender accounting — the very opposite of being forgotten.

9.text: Then my enemies will turn back on the day I call. This I know: God is for me.
9.amp: Then my enemies will turn back on the day I call [the moment trust becomes prayer, the tide begins to turn]. This I know [yada — I know it as settled fact]: God is for me [li — on my side, the preposition of belonging and partisanship].
9.notes: yada (H3045) = to know with certainty; the simple phrase 'God is for me' (Elohim li) is the bedrock confession of the psalm — echoed in Rom 8:31.

10.text: In God I praise His word; in the LORD I praise His word.
10.amp: In God [Elohim] I praise His word; in the LORD [YHWH] I praise His word [the same praise offered through both names — the God of all the earth is the covenant LORD of His servant].
10.notes: The repetition is deliberate: David boasts in God's word twice, once under the universal name Elohim and once under the covenant name YHWH — the same Word from the same God, anchoring the same trust.

11.text: In God I have placed my trust, and I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?
11.amp: In God I have placed my trust, and I will not be afraid. What can man [adam — mere earth-creature, dust returning to dust] do to me?
11.notes: The refrain returns from v.4, with one shift: 'flesh' (basar) becomes 'man' (adam). Same point, slightly broader scope — not just enemies in arms but any human threat at all.

12.text: Your vows are binding upon me, O God; I will render to You the offerings of thanksgiving.
12.amp: Your vows are binding upon me [neder — the promises I made to You, sealed before You, still owed], O God; I will render to You the offerings of thanksgiving [todah — the public thank-offering, declaring what You have done].
12.notes: neder (H5088) = a vow / solemn promise; todah (H8426) = thanksgiving / the thank-offering category in Lev 7. The trust of v.11 turns into liturgy: rescued men do not sneak away; they bring their thanks to the altar.

13.text: For You have snatched my soul out of death's grip — have You not also held my feet back from the fall — so that I may keep walking before God in the daylight of the living?
13.amp: For You have snatched my soul out of death's grip [natsal — pulled me from the very jaws]; have You not also held my feet back from the fall [dechi — the slip and stumble that would have finished me], so that I may keep walking before God in the daylight of the living [or hachayim — under His shining face, among those still alive in His care]?
13.notes: natsal (H5337) = to snatch away/rescue; dechi (H1762) = a stumble/falling; 'light of the living' (cf. Job 33:30) = the daylight of those still alive under God's care. The psalm ends not in safety alone but in vocation — David is rescued so he can keep walking, and his walking is now consciously before the face of God.
